For Flame in Freefall, I aim to combine scientific research with an engaging physics simulation. I'm looking for teammates skilled in physics, chemistry, web development, 3D modelling, animation, or scientific research. Most importantly, I value creativity, teamwork, and curiosity.
summary:
Flame in Freefall is an interactive website exploring how fire behaves in microgravity compared to Earth. It features scientific explanations, visual comparisons, an interactive physics simulation, and research from NASA experiments like SAFFIRE and ACME.

Users can adjust gravity, oxygen concentration, airflow, fuel supply, and temperature to see how these factors affect a simulated flame. This makes combustion science easier to explore through hands-on interaction.

The project highlights the importance of understanding fire in spacecraft, where enclosed environments make fire safety critical. By connecting interactive simulations with real space research, Flame in Freefall aims to make complex science accessible while showing how combustion research can help protect astronauts on future missions.
details:
Flame in Freefall is a browser-based interactive learning project that explores how fire behaves in microgravity compared to Earth. It uses visual comparisons, an environment switch, scientific explanations, and a research section covering NASA experiments such as SAFFIRE, ACME, FLEX, and SoFIE.

Users can switch between Earth and microgravity environments to observe the differences in flame appearance and understand how gravity affects convection and combustion. The website also includes a visualisation dashboard to introduce the kinds of measurements scientists study during combustion experiments. These visualisations are educational illustrations, not real-time NASA measurements or validated scientific simulations.

The project was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with browser-based visual elements and interactive features. No specialised hardware is required.

Its main benefit is making a complex scientific topic easier to understand without requiring advanced knowledge of physics or chemistry. The creative aspect is combining space science with an interactive website instead of presenting information through static text alone.

During development, we considered scientific accuracy, ease of use, visual clarity, accessibility, and the importance of distinguishing real NASA research from illustrative content. Our intended impact is to encourage curiosity about space science and help people understand why studying fire in microgravity is important for astronaut safety and future space missions.
